chief_complaint: multiple bruises and a patterned mark on the thigh
hpi_details: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother due to multiple bruises. The mother reports that he fell from the sofa yesterday. However, there is a delayed presentation, and her story changes when asked to repeat the details. On examination, the child has bruises on both ears, his back, and buttocks in various stages of healing (different colours). Notably, there is a patterned loop-shaped mark on his thigh. The child appears unusually quiet and withdrawn. Social history reveals that the mother's partner, who is not the biological father, cares for the child while she works night shifts.
ideas: Mother thinks the child is just clumsy and bruises easily.
concerns: Mother is worried she might get into trouble or be blamed for the injuries.
expectations: Mother expects a quick check-up and some ointment for the bruises so they can go home.
pmh: No history of bleeding disorders. Normal development.
social_hx: Lives with mother and her partner. Mother works night shifts. Mother's partner (not the biological father) looks after the child during the night.

boundaries_and_exceptions: In cases with known bleeding disorders, the threshold for bruising is lower, but patterned injuries still strongly suggest non-accidental trauma.
Certain cultural practices (e.g., coining, cupping) can cause unusual skin marks and must be carefully differentiated from physical abuse.
common_misconceptions: Believing that an abusive caregiver will always appear hostile or uncooperative.
Assuming that a single plausible explanation for one injury completely rules out abuse for all other injuries.
Hesitating to report suspicions of child abuse due to a lack of absolute, definitive proof.
Thinking that normal coagulation studies definitively rule out all non-abusive causes without considering the entire clinical picture.
core_concepts: Prompt recognition of suspicious injury patterns (e.g., patterned marks, bruises on atypical locations like ears, back, and buttocks) is essential for identifying non-accidental trauma.
Discrepancies between the provided history, the developmental age of the child, and the severity or mechanism of the injuries are major red flags.
The clinician's primary responsibility is ensuring the immediate safety of the child, which often necessitates admission if safety cannot be guaranteed at home.
Mandatory reporting to child protection agencies and the police is a strict legal obligation for clinicians when abuse is suspected.
dangerous_errors: Discharging the child back to a potentially dangerous environment without conducting a full safety assessment and making a mandated report.
Failing to perform a complete, head-to-toe skin examination to identify all hidden or occult injuries.
Taking an accusatory or confrontational tone with the caregiver, which may escalate the situation or cause them to flee with the child.
Neglecting to evaluate for internal or occult injuries (e.g., via skeletal survey or head imaging) in a young child with suspected physical abuse.
diagnostic_clues: Atypical bruise locations for a toddler (both ears, back, and buttocks).
Multiple bruises in various stages of healing (indicated by different colours).
Presence of a patterned injury, such as a loop-shaped mark on the thigh.
Inconsistent and changing history that does not plausibly explain the mechanism of injury.
Delayed presentation for medical care and the child's unusually quiet and withdrawn demeanour.
management_principles: Take a comprehensive, non-accusatory, and objective history from the caregivers.
Perform a full skin examination, document all injuries precisely, and admit the child to the hospital to ensure immediate safety.
Initiate a diagnostic workup including a skeletal survey, complete blood count (CBC), and coagulation panel.
Consider head imaging (e.g., non-contrast CT) given the risk of occult head trauma, especially with bruises on the ears.
Make a mandatory immediate report to the police (112) and the national child protection agency, and ensure the safety of any siblings in the home.

source_refs.title: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP): Clinical Report on the Evaluation of Suspected Child Physical Abuse

clinical_knowledge.topic: Evaluation and management of suspected physical child abuse

reference_soap.assessment: Suspected physical child abuse (non-accidental injury), supported by the presence of patterned marks, atypical bruise locations, multiple stages of healing, and an inconsistent history.
reference_soap.objective: Vital signs are stable. The child appears unusually quiet, withdrawn, and avoids eye contact. A full head-to-toe skin examination reveals bruises on both ears, the back, and buttocks in various stages of healing (different colours). A distinct, patterned loop-shaped mark is present on the right thigh. No active bleeding or other gross abnormalities noted on the general physical exam.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Admit the patient to the pediatric ward to ensure immediate safety. 2. Order a complete skeletal survey to evaluate for occult fractures. 3. Send blood for CBC and coagulation studies to rule out underlying bleeding disorders. 4. Consider a non-contrast head CT due to the bruises on the ears and risk of intracranial injury. 5. File a mandatory report with the police (112) and the child protection agency. 6. Assess and ensure the safety of any siblings living in the home. 7. Maintain a professional, non-accusatory approach with the caregivers throughout the evaluation.
reference_soap.subjective: 3-year-old boy brought to the emergency department by his mother due to multiple bruises. The mother claims he fell from the sofa yesterday, but her story changes upon re-questioning. There is a delay in seeking medical care. The mother works night shifts, and her partner cares for the child during that time. The child has no history of bleeding disorders and has normal development.

learning_objectives: Recognize red flags for physical child abuse, including patterned injuries, atypical bruise locations, and inconsistent histories.
Demonstrate a non-accusatory and objective approach to history-taking when child abuse is suspected.
Formulate an appropriate initial diagnostic workup for suspected child physical abuse, including a skeletal survey and screening laboratory tests.
Understand the legal and ethical obligations of clinicians as mandated reporters to notify child protection agencies and the police.

differentials: Bleeding disorder (e.g., Hemophilia, von Willebrand disease)

must_ask.objective: Establish the exact mechanism of injury reported by the caregiver
must_ask.say: Can you tell me exactly how he got these bruises on his body?

must_ask.objective: Identify discrepancies by asking for clarification
must_ask.say: Could you walk me through the fall from the sofa one more time so I make sure I have all the details correct?

must_ask.objective: Inquire about the presence of other caregivers
must_ask.say: Who was watching him when this happened?
Has he ever had excessive bleeding or does anyone in the family bruise easily?
Has he been acting differently or more quiet than his usual self recently?

must_ask.objective: Determine the safety of other children in the home
must_ask.say: Are there any other children living at home with you?

must_ask.objective: Explain the need for admission for safety
must_ask.say: We need to admit him to the hospital today to make sure he is safe and to run some tests.

teaching.one_liner: 3-year-old boy presenting with unexplained patterned bruising, atypical injury locations in various stages of healing, and an inconsistent history from the caregiver.
red_flags: Bruises on both ears, back, and buttocks
Bruises in various stages of healing

history.answer: I brought my son in because he fell off the sofa yesterday and has several bad bruises.
He was jumping around on the living room sofa yesterday afternoon and fell onto the floor.
Well, he might have fallen off the bed earlier this week instead, or maybe he tripped over some toys while playing.
I thought the marks would fade on their own, but this morning they looked darker and more noticeable.
I noticed that curved line on his thigh this morning, and I figured he must have landed hard on an electrical wire or toy.
He has marks on his back, his bottom, and around his ears, but he is constantly bumping into furniture.
He flinches a little if someone presses on his thigh, but otherwise he just stays quiet.
No, he did not lose consciousness, and he has not vomited or seemed confused.
No, nothing has ever touched or squeezed his neck.
He seems to get new bruises every week or two, but toddlers are just clumsy at this age.
I work night shifts at a convenience store, so my partner looks after him at home during the night.
They usually get along, though my partner gets frustrated and stressed when the boy will not stop crying.
My partner can get loud and has a temper when drinking, but he insists he would never hurt my boy.
He is my only child, so there are no other children living in our home.
No, he has never had any pain, bleeding, or redness around his private area.
No, he has never been given alcohol or swallowed any unknown medications.
He used to run around and laugh a lot, but lately he has been very clingy, quiet, and withdrawn.
He wakes up crying during the night and gets startled very easily by loud voices or sudden movements.
No, he has never had frequent nosebleeds, gum bleeding, or blood in his stool or urine.
No one in our family has hemophilia, platelet problems, or any bleeding condition.
He has had standard toddler colds, but he has never been diagnosed with any serious medical conditions.
He has never had any surgeries and has never been admitted to a hospital.
He does not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter syrups, or herbal remedies.
He has no known allergies to medicines, foods, or adhesives.
He was born at full term without any birth injuries or newborn complications.
He has met all of his milestones on time, like walking before his first birthday.
All of his childhood vaccinations are up to date at the community health clinic.
He stays at home and does not attend daycare, babysitters, or nursery school.
I think he is just naturally clumsy and bruises more easily than other kids his age.
I am worried people will judge me and think I am neglectful or that I will get into trouble.
I was hoping the doctor could just look at him quickly and give us some bruise ointment so we can go home.

exam.finding: Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse is 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, blood pressure is 96/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
A well-nourished 3-year-old boy who appears withdrawn, unusually quiet, and avoids eye contact with examiners.
Multiple ecchymoses in various healing stages on the back and buttocks, and a distinct loop-shaped patterned mark on the right thigh.
Ecchymoses on both ear pinnae without laceration, and tympanic membranes are intact without hemotympanum.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light, with no subconjunctival hemorrhage or periorbital swelling.
No chest wall deformity, rib cage tenderness, or bony crepitus noted on palpation.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender without palpable masses or organomegaly.
Normal active and passive range of motion across all extremities without joint swelling or focal bony tenderness.
Normal male external genitalia with no erythema, swelling, laceration, or discharge.
